sweep_summary: Anal (anal1239) is not in the catalog. The search of works with stress or accent in the title produced a single hit, Ozerov 2021 (Glossa, open access), which was already saved held by the project under and was re-read in full from the saved PDF/text. It is an intonation study of two IU-level pragmatic contours (Response-Seeking rise-fall on the IU-final syllable; Prosodic Intensification on one item within the IU) and contains no statement of where word stress falls; its only word-level prosodic content is that Anal has two lexical tones (high vs falling-low) with tone-assignment rules, citing Ozerov 2018 (Studies in Language, doi:10.1075/sl.17030.oze, paywalled, no OA copy), and it says the prosodic system 'requires further research' (pp. 3-4). Relevance: prosody-but-not-word-stress; bears_on_catalog: no-catalog-record; nothing to acquire (priority none). No first-hand word-stress statement for Anal was found in this search of works with stress in the title (the best new statement.nothing found); our earlier reading note in likewise records no stress/accent statement in Devi 2015, Ozerov 2019, Angom 2014, Thajamanbi 2015, Luwang 2022 or LSI III.3. a dated search line was appended to

new_statements.rule_in_words: Anal is described as a lexical tone language with two tones (Devi: high vs low; Ozerov 2019: High vs Low; Ozerov 2021: high vs falling-low, plus a vowel-length contrast, lexical stems carrying inherent tone and affixes receiving tone by spreading/polarity). None of the descriptions read makes any statement about word stress or word-level accent; Ozerov 2021 adds that 'the prosodic system of the language requires further research' and uses 'accent' only for intonation-unit-level salience marking.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source read.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Ozerov 2019/2021: utterance-final particles are toneless and take the IU-final contour; long vowels in lexical roots are mostly high-toned and glottalized; Greenhills variety keeps final /aʔ/ vs /áː/.
new_statements.domain_note: Tone is lexical (syllable/morpheme domain). The only 'accent' discussed (Ozerov 2021) is an intonation-unit-final or IU-internal pragmatic salience mark (Response-Seeking, Prosodic Intensification), i.e. phrase-level, explicitly distinct from the lexical system. No word-domain stress statement exists in the sources read.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same language, Glottolog anal1239 (Ozerov calls it 'Anal Naga'). Devi 2015's data come from Chandel and Chakpikarong sub-divisions (Chingkhu, Kanan, Japhou, Chandel Christian, Khambathel; Akaphe, Khubi, Rungchang, Shalluk villages). Ozerov 2019 notes minor dialect variation (Greenhills area keeps a word-final /aʔ/ vs /áː/ contrast) but no separate glottocode is involved.

sources.citation: Ozerov, Pavel. 2021. Prosodic salience in Anal Naga: where non-arbitrariness, phaticity and engagement meet. Glossa: a journal of general linguistics 6(1): 41, 1-25. doi:10.5334/gjgl.967

sources.quote: There are short and long vowels in the language that distinguish two tones: high and falling-low. Lexical stems and some grammatical morphemes carry an inherent tone. Other grammatical morphemes are assigned a tone by rules that involve a combination of tonal polarity and spreading (Ozerov 2018). Utterance final particles have no inherent tone and exhibit the final prosodic contour. [...] The prosodic system of the language requires further research. A preliminary study of 200 examples of Intonation Unit (IU) final contours revealed an utterance terminating falling contour and a continuing-level contour, as well as the infrequent level elongated hesitation.
sources.locator: Section 2 'Language background and data', pp. 3-4 (PDF pp. 3-4); the two contours RS and PI are described in Sections 3-4
sources.note: Nothing about word-stress placement. The paper is about two Intonation-Unit-level contours: a Response-Seeking contour (a 'strongly accented rise-fall on the last syllable of the Intonation Unit') and Prosodic Intensification (a deviant strong accent / extra-high pitch or falsetto / extreme rhyme lengthening on one lexical item within the IU). 'Accent' in the title-keyword sense here means utterance-level pragmatic prominence that overrides lexical tone, not a lexical/word-level stress system.
